name: Approve a CSR + fix a broken binding
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration. Drill EVERY RBAC corner harder than the exam: namespaced Role vs cluster-scoped ClusterRole, binding to users and ServiceAccounts, reusing a ClusterRole inside one namespace via a RoleBinding, least-privilege with resourceNames, apiGroups for subresources, approving a CSR, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Approve a CertificateSigningRequest
questions.teach:
A **CertificateSigningRequest** lets an admin issue a client cert to a new user. List pending ones with `kubectl get csr`, then grant one with `kubectl certificate approve <name>`; its condition then reads `Approved,Issued`.

**Gotcha:** approval only proves identity — it grants **no** permissions without a Role/ClusterRole binding.
questions.prompt:
The CSR `learn-dev` is already submitted and **Pending**. Approve it.

Target: `kubectl get csr learn-dev` shows condition `Approved,Issued`.
questions.hint: `kubectl get csr` to see it Pending, then `kubectl certificate approve learn-dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl get csr
kubectl certificate approve learn-dev
kubectl get csr learn-dev   # Approved,Issued
questions.eli5:
Imagine a new employee shows up and wants a building ID badge. They can't just print their own — they fill out an application and hand it to the security office. The office looks at it and either stamps **APPROVED** (and the badge machine spits out a real badge) or stamps **DENIED**.

A **CertificateSigningRequest (CSR)** is exactly that application. Someone generated a key and a request ("please sign this so I can be user `dev`") and submitted it. It's sitting there marked **Pending**, waiting for an admin.

You're the admin. You:

1. Look at the pile of applications: `kubectl get csr`
2. Stamp this one approved: `kubectl certificate approve learn-dev`

Now its status reads **Approved,Issued** — the certificate has been signed and handed back. The person can use it to *log in as* `dev`.

But here's the crucial part: a badge only proves **who you are** — it does not unlock any doors. Having the badge for `dev` lets the cluster recognize you as `dev`, and nothing more. What `dev` is actually allowed to *do* still depends entirely on Roles and RoleBindings (the previous lab).

**Watch out for:**

- **Approval grants ZERO permissions.** Identity ≠ authorization. Without a Role/RoleBinding, `dev` can log in and do absolutely nothing.
- You can **approve** or **deny** (`kubectl certificate deny <name>`) — once decided, you can't flip it; you'd delete and resubmit.
- After approval the signed cert lives in the CSR's `status.certificate` (base64) — the requester pulls it from there.
- A CSR needs a `signerName` (usually `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client` for user certs). Wrong signer, and it won't issue even after approval.
questions.deepDive:
## Approving a CertificateSigningRequest — full rundown

### The mental model
A **CSR** is how a new client gets an x509 client certificate signed by the cluster CA so the API server will **authenticate** it. The flow is: *generate key + CSR → submit to the API → admin approves → a signer issues the cert → client downloads and uses it*. Approval proves **identity only** — it grants **no permissions**. Authorization is a completely separate step (Role/RoleBinding).

### End-to-end flow
```bash
# 1) user generates a private key + a CSR (CN becomes the username, O becomes groups)
openssl genrsa -out dev.key 2048
openssl req -new -key dev.key -out dev.csr -subj "/CN=dev/O=devs"

# 2) base64 the CSR and submit a CertificateSigningRequest object
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  name: learn-dev
spec:
  request: $(base64 -w0 dev.csr)          # base64 of the PEM CSR
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client
  usages: ["client auth"]
  # expirationSeconds: 86400               # optional, >= 600
EOF

# 3) admin reviews + approves
kubectl get csr
kubectl certificate approve learn-dev

# 4) retrieve the signed cert
kubectl get csr learn-dev -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > dev.crt
```

### The commands
| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `kubectl get csr` | list CSRs + their condition |
| `kubectl get csr <name> -o yaml` | inspect request/signer/status |
| `kubectl certificate approve <name>` | approve → condition `Approved,Issued` |
| `kubectl certificate deny <name>` | deny → condition `Denied` |
| `kubectl describe csr <name>` | human-readable detail |

### CSR conditions
| Condition shown | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Pending` | awaiting an admin decision |
| `Approved,Issued` | approved **and** the signer issued the cert |
| `Approved` (no Issued) | approved but signer hasn't issued (wrong/unknown signer) |
| `Denied` | rejected |

### Well-known signerNames
| signerName | Purpose | usages |
|---|---|---|
| `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client` | general client certs (users) | `client auth` |
| `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet` | kubelet client certs | `client auth` |
| `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` | kubelet serving certs | `server auth` |
| `kubernetes.io/legacy-unknown` | legacy (not auto-issued) | — |

### Identity → authorization (the two halves)
1. **Authentication** (this lesson): the signed cert proves you are `CN=dev`, group `O=devs`.
2. **Authorization** (RBAC): bind a Role/ClusterRole to user `dev` (or group `devs`) to grant actual permissions.
```bash
kubectl config set-credentials dev --client-key=dev.key --client-certificate=dev.crt --embed-certs
# then a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding to user "dev" — otherwise dev can do nothing
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Approval ≠ permissions.** A freshly approved user has an identity and zero authorization until you bind a role.
- `kubectl certificate approve/deny` acts on the **CSR name**, not the username.
- The **CN** in the CSR subject becomes the **username**; each **O** becomes a **group** — bind RBAC to either.
- Wrong/missing **signerName** → it may show `Approved` but never `Issued`.
- A decision is terminal: you can't re-approve a denied CSR — delete and resubmit.
- `spec.request` must be the **base64 of the PEM CSR**; `usages` must include `client auth` for user certs.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl get csr                      # find the Pending one
kubectl certificate approve learn-dev
kubectl get csr learn-dev            # CONDITION: Approved,Issued
# remember: still needs a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding to do anything
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a binding that grants nothing
questions.teach:
When `auth can-i` says `no` despite a RoleBinding existing, suspect a **dangling roleRef**: the binding points at a Role name that doesn't exist, so it grants nothing silently. Check with `kubectl -n <ns> describe rolebinding <name>`.

**Gotcha:** a RoleBinding's `roleRef` is **immutable** — to repoint it you must delete and recreate the binding.
questions.prompt:
User `auditor` should be able to `get,list` `secrets` in `rbac-learn`, but `kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=auditor -n rbac-learn` returns `no`. A Role `secret-reader` (correct rules) and a RoleBinding `auditor-sr` already exist — the binding is misconfigured. Diagnose and fix it so `auditor` can list secrets. Don't change the Role's rules; fix the wiring.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=auditor -n rbac-learn` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n rbac-learn describe rolebinding auditor-sr` — its `roleRef` points at a Role that doesn't exist. Since roleRef is immutable, delete and recreate: `kubectl -n rbac-learn delete rolebinding auditor-sr` then `kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding auditor-sr --role=secret-reader --user=auditor`.
questions.solution:
# describe shows roleRef -> Role 'secret-readr' (typo); no such Role, so it grants nothing.
kubectl -n rbac-learn delete rolebinding auditor-sr
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding auditor-sr --role=secret-reader --user=auditor
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=auditor -n rbac-learn   # -> yes

verification.description: auditor can list secrets in rbac-learn (dangling roleRef fixed)

questions.eli5:
Picture the hire letter again: a **RoleBinding** staples a person to a job description (a Role). The staple has two ends — one end names the *person*, the other names the *job description by its exact title*.

Now imagine someone typed the job title wrong on the letter: it says "staple `auditor` to the job called **secret-readr**." But the actual job on the wall is called **secret-reader**. There is no job named `secret-readr`, so the letter points at *nothing*. The staple exists, it looks official, `auditor` thinks they're hired — but it connects them to empty air. Result: `auditor` can do nothing, and no error is ever shown. The security desk just keeps answering `no`.

To find it, you read the letter closely: `kubectl -n rbac-learn describe rolebinding auditor-sr` and look at the `roleRef` — it names a Role that doesn't exist.

Here's the painful twist: the "which job" end of the staple (`roleRef`) is **set in permanent ink** — you cannot edit it. The only fix is to throw the letter away and write a fresh one pointing at the correct job title.

So: delete the broken RoleBinding, recreate it pointing at the real Role `secret-reader`, and now `auditor` can list secrets.

**Watch out for:**

- A **dangling roleRef fails silently** — the binding exists, `auth can-i` just says `no` with no error. Always `describe` the binding and verify the Role it names actually exists.
- `roleRef` is **immutable** — you cannot `kubectl edit` it. You must **delete and recreate** the binding.
- Don't "fix" it by changing the Role's rules — the Role is fine; the *wiring* is wrong.
- Also double-check the **subject** end (name/kind) and that you're in the **right namespace** — the same silent failure happens if the user name is misspelled.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix a binding that grants nothing — full rundown

### The mental model
A RoleBinding has two linkage points: a **`roleRef`** (which Role/ClusterRole, by kind + name) and **`subjects`** (who). RBAC is allow-only and **fails open to "no"**: if *either* end doesn't resolve — the referenced role doesn't exist, or the subject name/kind is wrong — the binding grants nothing and produces **no error**. `kubectl auth can-i` just returns `no`. Diagnosis is a matter of inspecting all three links: role rules, roleRef, and subjects.

### The debugging workflow
```bash
# 1) Confirm the symptom
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=auditor -n rbac-learn      # -> no

# 2) Does the binding even exist, and what does it point at?
kubectl -n rbac-learn describe rolebinding auditor-sr
#   Role:        <roleRef kind/name>     <-- check this exists & matches
#   Subjects:    <kind/name/namespace>   <-- check name/kind/ns

# 3) Does the referenced Role exist (and have the right rules)?
kubectl -n rbac-learn get role secret-reader
kubectl -n rbac-learn describe role secret-reader   # verb/resource/apiGroup

# 4) Cross-check with the resolver
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=auditor -n rbac-learn --list
```

### Common RBAC failure modes
| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `can-i` = no, binding exists | **roleRef names a missing Role** (typo) | delete + recreate binding with correct `--role` |
| `can-i` = no, role is correct | subject **name/kind** wrong (`User` vs `ServiceAccount`, misspelled) | fix subjects (can `kubectl edit` subjects) |
| works in wrong ns | binding/role in the **wrong namespace** | recreate in the right `-n` |
| `get` works, `list` fails | **verb missing** from the Role rule | add verb to the Role |
| SA can't act | used `ns:name` in `--as` | use `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>` |
| cluster resource denied | used a **Role** for a cluster-scoped resource | switch to ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding |

### The immutable `roleRef`
`roleRef` cannot be changed after creation — the API server **rejects** any update to it:
```
the RoleBinding "auditor-sr" is invalid: roleRef: Invalid value: ... : cannot change roleRef
```
So the fix for a wrong roleRef is always **delete + recreate**:
```bash
kubectl -n rbac-learn delete rolebinding auditor-sr
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding auditor-sr \
  --role=secret-reader --user=auditor
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=auditor -n rbac-learn   # -> yes
```
> Note: **subjects** *are* mutable — you can `kubectl edit rolebinding` to add/fix subjects. Only `roleRef` requires recreation.

### Why a dangling roleRef is silent
RBAC authorization just evaluates every rule that *applies* to the subject. A binding whose roleRef resolves to no Role contributes **zero rules**. There's nothing to error on — the request simply isn't allowed by any rule, so the default-deny wins. No controller "repairs" or warns about dangling refs.

### Reading a describe output
```
Name:         auditor-sr
Role:
  Kind:  Role
  Name:  secret-readr          # <-- typo: no such Role exists -> grants nothing
Subjects:
  Kind  Name     Namespace
  ----  ----     ---------
  User  auditor
```
The mismatch between `Role.Name` here and the actual `kubectl get role` output is the smoking gun.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Dangling roleRef = silent no.** Always verify the referenced role **exists** with `kubectl get role/clusterrole`.
- `roleRef` is **immutable** → delete + recreate (do **not** waste time on `kubectl edit`).
- Don't "fix" by editing the Role's rules when the rules are correct — the wiring is the bug.
- Check **kind**: a RoleBinding's roleRef can be `Role` or `ClusterRole`; a ClusterRole reference needs `--clusterrole`, not `--role`.
- Check the **subject**: `User` vs `ServiceAccount` vs `Group`, exact name, and SA namespace.
- Check the **namespace**: a RoleBinding only works in its own namespace.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n rbac-learn describe rolebinding auditor-sr    # find the bad roleRef
kubectl -n rbac-learn delete rolebinding auditor-sr
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding auditor-sr --role=secret-reader --user=auditor
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=auditor -n rbac-learn   # yes
```
